messages.subject: refactor coupled_ode_system to use ode_system
parts:
Hi!

I intend to refactor the current coupled ode system object. For one reason I would like to align ODE codes (rk45 and bdf) and for two I would like to route execution through the ode_system object. The reason to do so is that we can plug into the system analytic Jacobians of the ODE wrt to states and parameters using partial template specialization's.

To illustrate what I mean, I prepared a "test" which has the sole purpose to show the execution time for the two cases (with AD and without AD):

https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/feature/issue-310-coupled_ode_system-refactor-only/test/unit/math/rev/mat/functor/integrate_ode_rk45_noAD_test.cpp

The speed gain for the specific case is close to 2x. This always depends on the ODE system, parameters, etc.. the speed gain will be larger for stiffer systems and for ODE systems with many states (this is my personal guess; the cases with many Jacobian evaluations). Applying this during model inference gave me 2-3x speedups.

Supplying the analytic Jacobians won't be something regular users will, rather only advanced users. Making this user friendly is a different topic (I can share some R codes which help already a lot).

I hold on for the moment with a pull request until the design is settled.

Best,
Sebastian

Hi Sebastian,

I think I see what's going on. Let me try to get everyone on board.

These are the three relevant files to look at:
  • oral_2cmt.hpp 
    The functor defined here is very close to what would be translated from Stan to C++.
  • ode_system.hpp
    The first functor is passed into this class, ode_system, to calculate Jacobians. Jacobians are required by CVODES. ode_system takes the functor and uses automatic differentiation to compute Jacobians. 
  • oral_2cmt_jacobian.hpp
    This is a template specialization of the second file, ode_system, but for the oral_2cmt functor. Here, the Jacobians are known analytically so they're computed using doubles and without automatic differentiation.
    This is a specialization for just that particular functor and is written in C++. This is currently not generated from the Stan language. In order to write analytic Jacobians in this way, a user needs to perform surgery on the generated code, but it can be done.
Some comments in no particular order:
  • I'm really pleased that autodiff is only 2x as long as putting in analytic gradients! That's awesome! I know this is a simpler example, but still... that's really rad.
  • I think there are changes we can make to ode_system to make things a lot better:
    • Rename. It's not an ode system. It's the Jacobians of an ode system. There are three functions exposed:
      1. A function to calculate the value of the ode at the time and state provided.
      2. A function to calculate the Jacobian of the RHS with respect to y.
      3. A function to calculate the Jacobians of the RHS with respect to y and the RHS with respect to theta.
    • Clean up the interface. I don't think it needs to be this complicated. For example, here are the three function signatures I would provide:
      std::vector<double> operator()(double t, const std::vector<double>& y). returns dy_dt.
      For the two Jacobian functions, I would simplify a lot and just use Eigen::Matrix<double, Dynamic, Dynamic> (or whatever the right type is). Having the indirection of Eigen::MatrixBase<Derived1> where Derived1 is a template parameter isn't helping. These things are double based containers and it would help a lot if it weren't overengineered. Unless there's a use-case that I'm missing. It doesn't look like there is, though.
    • I'd rethink cvodes_ode_data.hpp. I don't understand the naming. Now that I look at it, why aren't the functions in the existing ode_system.hpp renamed to rhs_sens() and dense_jacobian()? Would that be more descriptive?
  • What are your use cases for having people specify analytic Jacobians? (I guess CVODES is calling them sensitivities and dense Jacobians.)
    • If the goal is to have a user be able to hack the C++, I think it's sufficient to rename and clean up ode_system. And possibly cvodes_ode_data as well.
    • If the goal is to have people write sensitivities and dense Jacobians in the Stan language, then what do you expect it to generate? Right now, we don't even allow users to specify gradients on their own functions and I think this is a good thing. Experts will be able to get into the C++ directly. I think it's hard to implement gradients correctly and not allowing users to try has saved us a lot of effort.

I think I understand the tangle of ode classes now. I think it's much too complicated and that's why I was struggling with it. I'm sure we can simplify, if you want to go through with it.

Just to be clear, this change you're proposing has no affect on existing timing. It just allows you, an expert that's willing to hack the C++, to write analytic sensitivities and Jacobians, which, in this case, is a 2x speedup. (Or... does this speed up all of the odes in general? if so, I missed it and would like to know how / why.)



Daniel

On Friday, August 5, 2016 at 9:42:15 AM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
  • If the goal is to have people write sensitivities and dense Jacobians in the Stan language, then what do you expect it to generate? Right now, we don't even allow users to specify gradients on their own functions and I think this is a good thing. Experts will be able to get into the C++ directly. I think it's hard to implement gradients correctly and not allowing users to try has saved us a lot of effort.

I would place zero weight on the problems of users who specify their own gradients incorrectly, but I think we need to provide mechanisms to do this (correctly). Now there are more and more packages that do like rstanarm and provide a set of pre-compiled models or do like brms and generate Stan code that could benefit from something like this. Hacking the C++ in those cases is not a good option because it would have to be done programatically.

Another thing that ties into this is the Stan requirement that user-defined functions be defined. If you declare a function in the functions block but don't define it, then the parser throws an error even though the pre-processor would be perfectly happy to find it in another .cpp file or the linker would be perfectly happy to find it in a shared object. If the parser would just delete that check, then it would be a lot easier to utilize custom C++ that might accumulate analytical gradients or whatever.

Ben

Hi Daniel,

My main goal is to have ODEs in Stan at maximum speed. I fully agree that AD is amazingly fast! However, in my field (any I guess many others as well) I need to solve essentially the same ODE in many projects such that it is very reasonable to work out Jacobians for those often used ODE systems. For the current stage I just would like to have an easy C++ way to make the analytic Jacobians possible for ODEs. It is in fact not so magic to do this - there are lots of tools out there to do automatic code generation already. So it comes down to knowing these tools and a bit of copy and paste. No magic. That does not mean this should be worked on in the future, i.e. having some Stan language features which help users with this, but we need to go in steps here.

The change I have put up does two things:

1. Use the ode_system for calculating the Jacobians. Doing so enables that specifying analytic Jacobians once will be beneficial for bdf and rk45 integrators in Stan

2. I made the coupled_ode_system work with an unshifted sensitivity system. Up to now the shifting was done whenever the initials vary. However, this is not needed at all and I aligned this with the CVODES code. This may lead to a minor speedup, not sure.

To be clear on this - yes there is no speed gain of the rk45 integrator by now using the ode_system (if at all only a very minor).

You appear to be very confused by the naming of ode_system - we did have a discussion on stab-dev about this (https://groups.google.com/forum/m/?fromgroups#!searchin/stan-dev/ode_system$20name/stan-dev/Bi4D_2YSrjI). Bob and Michael supported the name for it. The design of the ode_system object was aligned with Bob who suggested to use function name overloading. I myself like the ode_system name - it does reflect that this is the ODE plus needed facilities which is the Jacobian in this case.

Now, ode_system should really only provide the Jacobian and not the sensitivity system. The reason is that with the Jacobian it is straightforward to generate the sensitivity system which is needed (which depends on the case var/double and var/double for inits and parameters). Moreover, the CVODES code needs the Jacobian wrt to the states to do its stiff integration. I am not sure if renaming to dense_jacobian makes sense for a Stan object. I mean CVODES makes the distinction between sparse and dense jacobians while Stan always gives you a dense version of it as far as I am aware. So changing to dense_jacobian the function calls - I don’t know.

Moreover, the need to use the MatrixBase Eigen functionality is coming from the fact that I can then pass into the function Matrix and Map objects. The Map functionality enables to write directly into memory chunks, this is used here:

https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/develop/stan/math/rev/mat/functor/cvodes_ode_data.hpp#L105

or here:

https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/feature/issue-310-coupled_ode_system-refactor-only/stan/math/rev/mat/functor/coupled_ode_system.hpp#L439

If you require a Matrix to be passed around then this leads to extra copies which have to be created. From my experience this leads to a ~2-5% performance degradation.

So here is what I would suggest to do:

1. We move the coupled_ode_system to use the ode_system AND to not anymore do a shifting operation (which is on the branch for feature 310)

2. We make cvodes_ode_data use the couple_ode_system which would then be possible as no more shifting is done. Now, this will lead to a minor performance hit for the bdf integrator whenever users supply the analytic Jacobians. The reason is that then the coupled_ode_system cannot be instructed to calculate only the sensitivity system, but not evaluate the function itself. As this is not the major use case of coupled_ode_system and probably the performance hit is not too large, this would be ok. This would lead to a removal of all the rhs_sens function floating around in cvodes_ode_data.

However, we will still need the cvodes_ode_data object around as this is needed for the CVODES integrator for the static callback. The name of the object stems from the CVODES notion here which refers to this callback „thing“ as user data.

Best,
Sebastian

    This is a template specialization of the second file, ode_system, but for the oral_2cmt functor. Here, the Jacobians are known analytically so they're computed using doubles and without automatic differentiation.

> >>
> >> The change I have put up does two things:
> >>
> >>
> >> 1. Use the ode_system for calculating the Jacobians. Doing so enables that specifying analytic Jacobians once will be beneficial for bdf and rk45 integrators in Stan
> >>
> >>
> >> 2. I made the coupled_ode_system work with an unshifted sensitivity system. Up to now the shifting was done whenever the initials vary. However, this is not needed at all and I aligned this with the CVODES code. This may lead to a minor speedup, not sure.

> >>
> >> To be clear on this - yes there is no speed gain of the rk45 integrator by now using the ode_system (if at all only a very minor).

> >>

Bob and Michael supported the name for it. The design of the ode_system object was aligned with Bob who suggested to use function name overloading. I myself like the ode_system name - it does reflect that this is the ODE plus needed facilities which is the Jacobian in this case.
> >>
> >>
> >> Here's the thread (the last link didn't go anywhere):
> >> https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/Bi4D_2YSrjI/ifd8mWKxBQAJ
> >>
> >>

> >>
> >>
> >> I would think F is the ode_system and what you're describing is a way to wrap F and get sensitivities. So I'd just prefer a much more descriptive name that doesn't overload what we take to be the existing ode_system.

I mean CVODES makes the distinction between sparse and dense jacobians while Stan always gives you a dense version of it as far as I am aware. So changing to dense_jacobian the function calls - I don’t know.

> >> In the integrator we have now, do we ever use both?

> >>
> >> (those are actual questions.... not sure what the answers are and if I'm missing something)

> >>

> >>

> >>

> >>
> >> I don't understand what this means. What is a "shifting operator"?
> >>
> >>
> >> What part of the coupled_ode_system needs to use the ode_system?

> >>
> >> Can we add a step 0 and rename ode_system? (Either that or give me a good name for the functor F, the system of ordinary differential equations.... if you tell me that's called something else in the literature, then I'll start referring to that as something else and we can leave this is "ode_system.")

> >> I think I see what's going on. Let me try to get everyone on board.

> >> These are the three relevant files to look at:
> >> oral_2cmt.hpp
> >> The functor defined here is very close to what would be translated from Stan to C++.
> >> ode_system.hpp
> >> The first functor is passed into this class, ode_system, to calculate Jacobians. Jacobians are required by CVODES. ode_system takes the functor and uses automatic differentiation to compute Jacobians. oral_2cmt_jacobian.hpp
> >> This is a template specialization of the second file, ode_system, but for the oral_2cmt functor. Here, the Jacobians are known analytically so they're computed using doubles and without automatic differentiation.
> >> This is a specialization for just that particular functor and is written in C++. This is currently not generated from the Stan language. In order to write analytic Jacobians in this way, a user needs to perform surgery on the generated code, but it can be done.
> >> Some comments in no particular order:
> >> I'm really pleased that autodiff is only 2x as long as putting in analytic gradients! That's awesome! I know this is a simpler example, but still... that's really rad.I think there are changes we can make to ode_system to make things a lot better:Rename. It's not an ode system. It's the Jacobians of an ode system. There are three functions exposed:
> >> 1. A function to calculate the value of the ode at the time and state provided.
> >> 2. A function to calculate the Jacobian of the RHS with respect to y.
> >> 3. A function to calculate the Jacobians of the RHS with respect to y and the RHS with respect to theta.Clean up the interface. I don't think it needs to be this complicated. For example, here are the three function signatures I would provide:
> >> std::vector<double> operator()(double t, const std::vector<double>& y). returns dy_dt.
> >> For the two Jacobian functions, I would simplify a lot and just use Eigen::Matrix<double, Dynamic, Dynamic> (or whatever the right type is). Having the indirection of Eigen::MatrixBase<Derived1> where Derived1 is a template parameter isn't helping. These things are double based containers and it would help a lot if it weren't overengineered. Unless there's a use-case that I'm missing. It doesn't look like there is, though.
> >> I'd rethink cvodes_ode_data.hpp. I don't understand the naming. Now that I look at it, why aren't the functions in the existing ode_system.hpp renamed to rhs_sens() and dense_jacobian()? Would that be more descriptive?What are your use cases for having people specify analytic Jacobians? (I guess CVODES is calling them sensitivities and dense Jacobians.)If the goal is to have a user be able to hack the C++, I think it's sufficient to rename and clean up ode_system. And possibly cvodes_ode_data as well.If the goal is to have people write sensitivities and dense Jacobians in the Stan language, then what do you expect it to generate? Right now, we don't even allow users to specify gradients on their own functions and I think this is a good thing. Experts will be able to get into the C++ directly. I think it's hard to implement gradients correctly and not allowing users to try has saved us a lot of effort.
> >>

> >> I think I understand the tangle of ode classes now. I think it's much too complicated and that's why I was struggling with it. I'm sure we can simplify, if you want to go through with it.

> >>
> >> Just to be clear, this change you're proposing has no affect on existing timing. It just allows you, an expert that's willing to hack the C++, to write analytic sensitivities and Jacobians, which, in this case, is a 2x speedup. (Or... does this speed up all of the odes in general? if so, I missed it and would like to know how / why.)
